compression.title: Jacket2
compression.lede: is an online magazine of commentary on modern and contemporary poetry and poetics at the Kelly Writers House, University of Pennsylvania, published by Al Filreis; it keeps the complete archive of John Tranter's Jacket (1997–2010) and signs each piece with the names of those who made it.

sentences.text: Jacket2 (J2) is an online magazine of commentary on modern and contemporary poetry and poetics, which publishes articles, reviews, interviews, discussions and collaborative responses, archival documents, podcasts, and descriptions of poetry symposia and projects.

It publishes content as it is ready, in its own phrase "Not unlike a daily news forum", and keeps an index of everything it has published; the encyclopedia's account says new material is added every day, and nothing in its saved pages calls it peer-reviewed.
Its unit is the piece, filed under the sections Articles, Features, Reviews, Interviews, Commentaries, Reissues, Podcasts, Poems and Galleries, each piece under the names of its author or authors.

Whether it publishes poetry is stated two ways: Wikipedia, "As of 2023", says it "does not publish poetry", while its own index lists a Poems section and its home page carries "a new poem by Michele Leggott".
The encyclopedia also reads it, under its own hedge, as a magazine that "primarily featured original content but also included material that was excerpted from or co-produced with other sources".

It is hosted by the Kelly Writers House at 3805 Locust Walk, Philadelphia, a programming and community space on the campus of the University of Pennsylvania that counts Jacket2 among the publications it sponsors or hosts.

The Writers House was founded in 1995 by Al Filreis with volunteers from the university's faculty, students, staff and alumni, is partially funded by the university's Provost's Office, and is the subject of a Jacket2 commentary by Filreis on its founding thirty years on.
Filreis, Kelly Family Professor of English and the Writers House's founder and faculty director, is the publisher of Jacket2 and keeps an ongoing commentary there.
Wikipedia names Jessica Lowenthal, director of the Writers House, as associate publisher, and Julia Bloch and Michael S. Hennessey as editors.

The home page signs a memorial to Alice Notley "Jacket2 Editors" and names an editorial assistant, Emi Wong Shing; its About page returned "The requested page could not be found." when the census saved it.

The census accordingly records its operator as Jacket2 at the Writers House address, with no editorial board named beyond the collective signature, and its holder as Jacket2, "© 2026 Jacket2", its Terms of Use unread and no license stated.

Jacket was founded in 1997 by John Tranter (1943–2023), an Australian poet, publisher and editor, as an internet quarterly, which he published and edited until 2010, when he gave it to the University of Pennsylvania.

Jacket2 maintains the complete archive of Jacket, forty issues from 1997 to 2010, and the encyclopedia calls it Jacket's "new incarnation", carrying the original "from a "2.0 mode" into an interactive magazine"; the census keeps the two apart, Jacket held as the archive Jacket2 keeps.
Its home page carries an interview with Tranter as Jacket's founder.
The year Jacket2 began is given differently by its sources.

Its home page celebrates a fifteenth birthday on April 5th, with no year, and offers one piece from each of its last fifteen years, under a footer of 2026; Wikipedia, to which the title redirects, describes it as an online literary magazine "(2010-)" and files it among magazines established in 2010; the census records the founding as not stated and the magazine as active.
The Capture Registry finds that the AI Mode answer's relaunch year, 2011, puts that birthday in 2026, a figure no source the census saved states.

It reissues seven small-press magazines and presses, each with its editors: Roof (1976–79, ed. James Sherry), New Wilderness Letter (1977–84, ed. Jerome Rothenberg), Infolio (1986–91, ed. Tom Raworth), M/E/A/N/I/N/G (1986–1996, ed. Susan Bee and Mira Schor), O Books (1988–2009, ed. Leslie Scalapino et al.), XCP: Cross Cultural Poetics (1997–2010, ed. Mark Nowak) and Aufgabe (2001–2014, ed. E. Tracy Grinnell et al.).

Its podcasts include PennSound podcasts, Sounding Translation and PennSound Rewind, and its home page lists PennSound's newest additions, PennSound's editors and curators being, in its words, "more or less constantly adding new materials to the archive".
The census reads it beside PennSound, which holds the recordings, and beside the Electronic Poetry Center, which links its obituaries and tributes.
Filreis co-founded PennSound with Charles Bernstein and co-directs it, "the world's largest archive of recordings of poets performing their work".

PoemTalk is "a collaboration of the Kelly Writers House and PennSound", produced and hosted by Filreis, with Zach Carduner as its engineer and editor, available on podcast platforms and numbered to #222 on the home page.
Each episode convenes guests around one poem or a few: Marianne Moore's "To a Giraffe" in #222, two poems by Genevieve Taggard in #220, three by Larry Eigner in #97.

Each piece stands under the names of those who made it: co-authors, interviewers and translators are named in the byline, as in "Uldis Bērziņš, translated by Kevin M. F. Platt and Sintija Ozoliņa", and one piece is signed collectively, "Jacket2 Editors".
Its media highlight credits the sculpture "God" as "Made collaboratively" by Morton Schamberg and Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven.
The saved pages state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names, and the census records that it holds each piece under the byline as published.

The census, whose question is how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, admits it as an aggregator, asks of it under whose names, singly, jointly or collectively, a piece of commentary on poetry is published, and files it under avant-garde and experimental archives as a peripheral comparator.
The archive reads Jacket2 as supporting criticism whose byline keeps translators, a collective editorial signature and a collaborative making as attributions of their own.

In the archive's typology of authorship, collaborative authorship, where several persons contribute to one authorial position, stands beside direct, pseudonymous and heteronymic authorship, and the law, the knowledge graph and the scholarly apparatus are held to accommodate each structure without collapsing it into direct authorship.

The archive distinguishes the pseudonym, which changes the label attached to an authorial function, from the heteronym, which changes the organization of the function itself, and sets ordinary translation, ordinary editing, institutional office-holding and collaborative authorship without a constituted heteronym outside heteronymy.

In its account of attribution regimes, the civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across scholarly, literary, institutional and platform-mediated production, and publishing contracts attach to legal names.

Its saved pages touch machine participation in authorship only in an excerpt presented at "Poets Confront AI and Surveillance Capitalism", curated by William Lessard at Poets House, New York, on April 7, 2026; the archive finds no essay among them on how authorship is made or attributed with machine participation.

Its method is the editorial publication of commissioned and submitted commentary as it is ready, the reissue of small-press magazines and podcast production with PennSound, over modern and contemporary poetry, with reissued magazines from 1976 and Jacket from 1997.

Read through the census, it answers what it has published on a poet, book or small press and under whose byline, and whether a reissued magazine or an issue of Jacket is in its archive; it leaves unanswered its editorial policy and editors, its handling of a pseudonym or heteronym, and the rights of its reissues and of the Jacket archive.

Wikipedia's account of it is a section of the article on the Kelly Writers House, an article flagged as relying excessively on primary sources, and names contributors including Rachel Blau DuPlessis, Kristin Prevallet and Marjorie Perloff; the article on Tranter, flagged as needing more citations, cites for its lead a Jacket2 page titled "About us", retrieved 18 January 2024.
The archive's lexical engine names Jacket2, with electronic book review, as a literary-theory venue for essays on training-layer literature, retrocausal canon formation and the digital heteronym.

The archive's critical edition of Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose takes Kerouac's "Belief & Technique for Modern Prose" from Al Filreis's post at Jacket2, among the external sources verified for the edition.

Asked for "Jacket2", the census name and a new address, in Google AI Mode, signed out, on 1 November 2026, the composition described the magazine, its host, the journal it succeeds and the editors of the relaunch, then four kinds of content, and asked what the user wanted next, with no source card under the answer.
The Capture Registry finds the succession from Jacket composed at its grain, the forty issues agreeing with the archive's issue list.

It finds the University of Pennsylvania and two co-editors named with no card, the archive's span given as "late 20th and early 20th-century", the reissues of magazines and presses composed as "out-of-print poetry books", and the byline the census reads Jacket2 for left unsaid.

In the archive's account, an adequate answer about a work keeps apart whether its maker exists, whether it happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, names the object at its own level, and shows the evidence for it and where that evidence comes from.

CAP-1-01.quote: THE SUCCESSION AT ITS GRAIN. 'Jacket, which was originally founded and edited by poet John Tranter in 1997' and 'When Tranter retired from the publication in late 2010, the magazine's archive and continuation were transferred to the University of Pennsylvania'. The home page: 'We maintain the complete archive of Jacket magazine, founded and edited by John Tranter.' and 'Jacket 1997–2010'. The composition's 'all 40 original issues' agrees with the archive's issue list, which ends '36 37 38 39 40 © 2026 Jacket2'.

CAP-1-06.quote: The magazine composed at its grain, its succession from Jacket stated as the home page states it, with a relaunch year that dates the census's undated fifteenth birthday. The host and editors come with no card, and the byline practice the census row reads it for is absent.

CAP-1-03.quote: THE HOST AND THE EDITORS BEYOND THE SAVED PAGES. The census row's operator is Jacket2 at the address in its footer, 'Kelly Writers House 3805 Locust Walk Philadelphia, PA 19104-6150', with no editorial board beyond pieces signed 'Jacket2 Editors' ('In Memoriam: Alice Notley (1945–2025) Jacket2 Editors'); its About page returned 'The requested page could not be found.' The composition names the University of Pennsylvania and 'the co-editing direction of Al Filreis and Jessica Lowenthal' with no card; the X result above the answer carries 'Affiliated with the Kelly Writers House at the University of Pennsylvania.'

CAP-1-04.quote: THE ARCHIVE'S CENTURY AND ITS REISSUES. 'maintaining an irreplaceable archive of late 20th and early 20th-century poetry networks': the second term repeats the first century, where the archive's span, 'Jacket 1997–2010', runs into the twenty-first. 'Digital reissues of rare out-of-print poetry books': the home page's reissues are magazines and presses, 'Roof, 1976–79 (ed. James Sherry)', 'XCP: Cross Cultural Poetics, 1997–2010 (ed. Mark Nowak)', 'Aufgabe, 2001–2014 (ed. E. Tracy Grinnell et al.)', each with its editors.

CAP-1-05.quote: THE BYLINE NOT CARRIED. The census reads Jacket2 for how its pages sign: translators in the byline ('Uldis Bērziņš, translated by Kevin M. F. Platt and Sintija Ozoliņa'), a collective signature ('Jacket2 Editors'), a construction 'Made collaboratively from Philadephia-born artist Morton Schamberg and German baroness Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven'. The composition gives 'multi-author feature portfolios' and PoemTalk's 'panel of poets and scholars' and says nothing of how a piece is signed.
